content: The implementation of infection-control practices in dentistry should be guided by recommendations issued by local, state, or federal environmental regulatory agencies. It is essential to ensure consistent adherence to these recommended infection-control strategies. This includes the use of protective barriers and the proper sterilization or disinfection of instruments and environmental surfaces. Every dental facility must establish a written protocol that outlines procedures for instrument reprocessing, operatory cleanup, and the management of occupational injuries. All dental healthcare workers (DHCWs) should receive comprehensive training in proper infection-control practices. This training should begin during their professional or vocational education and be regularly updated through continuing education programs. Efforts to protect both patients and DHCWs should focus on enhanced surveillance, thorough risk assessment, evaluation of preventive measures to reduce exposure, and research into post-exposure prophylaxis. These initiatives could lead to the development of safer and more effective medical devices, work practices, and personal protective equipment. Such advancements should be acceptable to DHCWs, practical, cost-effective, and should not compromise the quality of patient care. In dentistry, there is a need for additional research to accurately assess factors that may increase the risk of transmitting bloodborne pathogens and other infectious agents in dental settings. Studies should investigate the nature, frequency, and circumstances of occupational exposures. This information could facilitate the development and evaluation of improved designs for dental instruments, equipment, and personal protective devices. Furthermore, the design of future dental instruments and equipment should incorporate more efficient reprocessing techniques to enhance infection control and safety.
